title: Disturbing Student Behaviors That Warrant Immediate Referral
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Beyond legal obligations to report suspected abuse, Linsin identifies a category of students who need professional referral to administrators, counselors, or psychologists but often get overlooked because attention goes to disruptive students instead. He outlines four broad, non-diagnostic categories of concerning behavior: disconnected students who move and speak in a flat, dreamlike, unaware manner; withdrawn students who hide behind clothing, avoid speech, and isolate themselves; threatening students who show violent themes in stories, drawings, or cruelty toward animals even without overt threats; and bizarre students whose speech or behavior seems disturbingly mismatched to the situation. He stresses that teachers are not meant to diagnose but simply to notice and escalate through documentation and direct communication with stakeholders, framing the responsibility as potentially life-saving.
points: Disruptive students often get referred while quietly struggling students, who need real professional help, are overlooked.
Disconnected students show flat, dreamlike, monotone behavior seemingly unaware of their surroundings.
Withdrawn students hide behind clothing, speak rarely, and isolate themselves from peers.
Threatening signs include violent drawings, obsession with weapons, and cruelty toward animals, even without overt threats.
Teachers should notice and escalate through email documentation and direct conversation with stakeholders, not attempt to diagnose.
quotes: Make no mistake, there is a substantial segment of students—growing by the day—that need professional help but are overlooked.
Disruptive students, who need nothing more than good, solid classroom management, get referred all the time.
They appear as if they’re in a dream, seemingly unaware of those around them.
Violent stories, drawings, sketches, and diagrams. Unusual obsession with weapons or brutality. Glimpses of rage. Mentions of cruelty or harm toward animals.
But a student experiencing a real mental health crisis needs serious intervention, of the kind you and maybe not even your school can provide.
Observe. Ask questions. Raise the alarm. Send an email first for documentation and then voice your concern personally to all stakeholders.
